newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks take beating on strong economic data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks take beating on strong economic data.

text.p: Stocks took a beating on Friday, trading near session lows after unexpectedly strong economic data tripped up the bond market and gave investors an excuse to take profits in stocks.
At 1 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT), the Dow Jones industrial average was down 98.95 points, or 1.2 percent, at 8,123.66. Decliners dominated advancers by a 20-8 margin on volume of 299 million shares.
The Nasdaq composite slid 6.95 points, or 0.44 percent, to 1,586.86 points.

The bellwether 30-year Treasury bond, whose lower yields have recently propelled stocks higher, sank 1-26/32, or $18.125 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield to 6.44 percent from Thursday's close of 6.30 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The markets stumbled because the July employment report and the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index, revived lurking inflation fears, analysts said.

"We got low unemployment, jobs creation and a strong NAPM figure," said Robert Froelich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "The combination of these numbers, even if there was no sign of wage inflation, caused the stock market to think about the risk of higher rates."
Bonds and stocks started their downward spiral after 10 a.m. EDT (1400 GMT), when the NAPM reported its index of manufacturing activity read 58.6 in July, up from 55.7 in June.
The closely watched price component, which is an indicator of manufacturing sector pricing pressures, rose to 53.6 for the month from 48.1 in June.
The group said the overall index rose to its highest level in 2-1/2 years, while the production indicator hit the strongest level in more than 9-1/2 years.
"The rise in the prices paid knocked the bond market down and brought some profit-taking into the stock market," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
The strong manufacturing data cast a pall over financial markets while they were sifting through the critical July employment report.

The Labour Department reported nonfarm payrolls grew by 316,000 in July, compared with a revised 228,000 jobs in June and a forecast gain of 193,000 jobs. The unemployment rate dropped to 4.8 percent from 5.0 percent, its lowest level in 24 years.

"The markets did not like all the information about the economy doing better," said Alfred Kugel, Stein Roe & Farnham senior investment strategist. "The increase in employment and improvement in manufacturing provided an excuse to sell."

But while bonds eased on the employment data, stocks held small gains until the NAPM data was released. Some analysts said the jobs data was not as strong as it appeared because average hourly wages were steady and the work week declined.
Both bonds and stocks had also been vulnerable to profit-taking, after staging a powerful advance in July.
"We're just giving back some of our recent gains," said Jim Benning, a trader at BT Brokerage.

Among particular issues, Kellogg Co. stock soared 4-13/16 to 96-11/16. It reported above-forecast second-quarter earnings of 83 cents per share, compared with 45 cents per share in the year-ago quarter. It said global sales volume rose 14 percent, excluding recently acquired Lender's Bagels.

Salomon Inc.'s stock firmed 2-8/16 to 66. It declined to comment on an article in Business Week magazine that it was viewed as a leading potential takeover target in Wall Street's ongoing wave of consolidation.
